summary: Registers the SASL mechanisms SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, gives guidance on implementing the original SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS securely, and updates the SCRAM registration procedures in RFC 5802.

plainLanguage.summary: SCRAM is a way for a program to prove it knows a password without ever sending the password over the network. This RFC registers the versions of SCRAM that use a stronger hash function, and it tightens the rules for the variants that tie the login to the encrypted connection it runs over.

questions: what is the minimum scram iteration count
how does scram-sha-256 differ from scram-sha-1
subtitle: A short RFC that adds SHA-256 versions of the SCRAM password login and tightens the rules for using channel binding safely.

tldr.problem: The SCRAM login mechanisms in RFC 5802 were built on SHA-1, and after RFC 5802 was published it was found that TLS does not have the properties the tls-unique channel binding needs in order to be secure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, defined exactly like the SHA-1 versions except that the hash function for HMAC() and H() is SHA-256, and it adds a rule for using the -PLUS mechanisms safely over TLS.
tldr.outcome: SHA-256 has stronger security properties than SHA-1, and the RFC expects SCRAM mechanisms based on it to have greater predicted longevity. The RFC also updates the SCRAM registration procedures of RFC 5802 and was later updated by RFC 9266.

today: RFC 7677 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5802, and it was itself updated by RFC 9266. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a SHA-256 Version of SCRAM
sections.content:
This document registers two SASL mechanisms, SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS. SASL is the Simple Authentication and Security Layer, the framework a protocol uses when it needs to check who is at the other end before letting a conversation start. SHA-256 has stronger security properties than SHA-1, and the RFC expects SCRAM mechanisms based on it to have greater predicted longevity than the ones based on SHA-1.

The registration form for the SCRAM family of algorithms is also updated from RFC 5802.

There was a second reason for the document. After RFC 5802 was published, it was discovered that Transport Layer Security (TLS), described in RFC 5246, does not have the expected properties for the "tls-unique" channel binding to be secure. Channel binding is the mechanism that ties an authentication exchange to the encrypted channel it happens over, so that a stolen password cannot be replayed over a different channel. The RFC therefore contains normative text that applies to both the original SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS mechanism and the newly introduced SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The login method was sound, but the hash function underneath it was showing its age, so this RFC registers a stronger version. It also closes a gap that turned up after the original login method was published: the way some servers tied a login to its encrypted connection was not as safe as everyone assumed.

sections.title: What SCRAM-SHA-256 Changes
sections.content:
The RFC does not redefine SCRAM. The two new mechanisms are defined in the same way that SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS are defined in RFC 5802, except that the hash function for HMAC() and H() uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1, as specified in RFC 6234. The -PLUS variant is the one that uses channel binding; the plain variant is there for clients that do not support it.

One concrete parameter is set. The hash iteration-count announced by a server SHOULD be at least 4096. The GSS-API mechanism OID for SCRAM-SHA-256 is 1.3.6.1.5.5.18.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same login with the same steps. Only the hashing function inside is stronger, and the server is asked to repeat that hashing at least 4096 times before it answers.

sections.title: A SCRAM-SHA-256 Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC gives a simple SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication exchange for a client that does not support channel bindings, using the username user and the password pencil.

The client opens with the username and a random nonce, in the form n,,n=user,r=rOprNGfwEbeRWgbNEkqO. The server answers with its own extended nonce, a salt and the iteration count: r=rOprNGfwEbeRWgbNEkqO%hvYDpWUa2RaTCAfuxFIlj)hNlF$k0, s=W22ZaJ0SNY7soEsUEjb6gQ==, i=4096. The client then sends a channel-binding flag, the combined nonce and a proof: c=biws, r=..., p=dHzbZapWIk4jUhN+Ute9ytag9zjfMHgsqmmiz7AndVQ=. The server finishes with its own verification value: v=6rriTRBi23WpRR/wtup+mMhUZUn/dB5nLTJRsjl95G4=.

Across the four messages the password itself never appears. What travels is a nonce, a salt, an iteration count and two values computed from the password.
sections.plainLanguage: You and the server trade four short notes. Each note proves a bit more that you both know the secret, but the secret itself is never written on any of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations from RFC 5802 still apply. On top of that, the RFC sets one rule for the -PLUS mechanisms: to be secure, SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS MUST be used over a TLS channel that has had the session hash extension of RFC 7627 negotiated, or session resumption MUST NOT have been used. The RFC points at RFC 4270 and RFC 6194 for reasons to move from SHA-1 to a strong security mechanism like SHA-256.

The strength of the mechanism depends in part on the hash iteration-count, written i in RFC 5802. As a rule of thumb the iteration-count should be such that a modern machine will take 0.1 seconds to perform the complete algorithm. The RFC notes that this is unlikely to be practical on mobile devices and other relatively low-performance systems: at the time of writing the rule of thumb gives around 15,000 iterations, while a hash iteration-count of 4096 takes around 0.5 seconds on current mobile handsets.

The computational cost can be avoided by caching the ClientKey, assuming the Salt and the hash iteration-count are stable. The recommendation of the specification is therefore that the hash iteration-count SHOULD be at least 4096, but careful consideration ought to be given to using a significantly higher value, particularly where mobile use is less important.
sections.plainLanguage: The more times the server repeats the hashing, the harder it is for a thief to guess the password, but the slower things get on a phone. So the RFC sets a floor of 4096 and asks for more where the devices are not phones.

sections.title: Registering the SCRAM Family
sections.content:
Section 5.1 updates the registration of the SCRAM family in the SASL mechanism registry of RFC 4422. The email address for reviews is updated and the note at the end changes. Members of the family MUST be explicitly registered using the "IETF Review" procedure of RFC 5226, and reviews MUST be requested on the KITTEN mailing list. The intended usage is COMMON and the change controller is the IESG. A note is added for future designers: each new SASL SCRAM mechanism MUST be explicitly registered with IANA within the SASL SCRAM Family Mechanisms registry.

Section 5.2 adds a new IANA registry named "SASL SCRAM Family Mechanisms", which gives every member of the family two new fields: a minimum iteration-count and an associated OID. The existing entries for SASL SCRAM-SHA-1 and SASL SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS move from the existing SASL mechanism registry into the new one, with a minimum iteration-count of 4096 and the OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.14 that came from RFC 5802.

Two new mechanisms are added to the new registry. SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS both get a minimum iteration-count of 4096 and the OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.18. Only one OID is needed for a SCRAM-NAME and SCRAM-NAME-PLUS pair, and the same OID is given to both entries.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of every official login method. This RFC adds a proper shelf for the SCRAM family, moves the older entries onto it with their numbers, and puts the two new ones there too with a floor on how many times the hashing must be repeated.
